name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q01 - Instantaneous speed versus average speed relationships

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At any given instant of time, the instantaneous speed of an object in rectilinear motion is equal to the magnitude of its instantaneous velocity.

Statement II: Over any finite time interval, the average speed of an object moving along a straight line is always equal to the magnitude of its average velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Instantaneous velocity is defined as the derivative of position with respect to time, \(v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\), and instantaneous speed is the rate of change of distance with time. Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, \(\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\), while average speed is total path length divided by elapsed time, \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\text{Path length}}{\Delta t}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
As the time interval \(\Delta t\) approaches zero, the magnitude of the infinitesimal displacement \(|\Delta x|\) becomes identical to the infinitesimal path length \(\Delta s\). Consequently, instantaneous speed equals the magnitude of instantaneous velocity at every single instant. Thus, the first statement is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
Over a finite time interval, if a particle reverses its direction of motion along the straight line, the total path length traversed is strictly greater than the magnitude of displacement (\(\text{path length} > |\Delta x|\)). As a result, average speed is strictly greater than the magnitude of average velocity whenever reversal occurs. Thus, the claim that they are always equal over any finite interval is false. Hence, the second statement is incorrect.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
Evaluating both statements demonstrates that the first statement represents a universally valid kinematic principle, whereas the second statement fails for any motion involving reversal of direction. Therefore, the first statement is correct but the second statement is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

answer.text: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q02 - Scope of kinematics and point object model

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In kinematics, we investigate and describe the causes of motion and the dynamical forces responsible for acceleration.

Statement II: A spinning cricket ball that turns sharply upon striking the pitch can be accurately approximated as a point object.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes the motion of objects without going into the causes of motion (forces), which are instead studied in dynamics. A moving body can be approximated as a point object only when its linear dimensions are negligible compared to the distance it travels, and its internal rotational motions do not significantly influence the trajectory.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
Kinematics is purely descriptive of position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time; it explicitly does not examine the physical causes or forces producing the motion. The causes of motion form the subject matter of dynamics (Newton's laws of motion). Therefore, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
When a spinning cricket ball hits the ground and turns sharply, its rotational motion and physical size are critical to its deflection and interaction with the pitch. Because its rotation cannot be neglected and governs the abrupt deviation in direction, treating it as a point mass leads to significant error. Therefore, the second statement is incorrect.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
Both propositions mischaracterize foundational mechanics definitions: the first misdefines kinematics by including forces, and the second misapplies the point object approximation to a body whose rotational dynamics dominate its behavior. Therefore, both statements are incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q03 - Acceleration signs and apex instantaneous velocity

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A particle moving with a positive acceleration must always experience an increase in its speed.

Statement II: A particle thrown vertically upward has zero instantaneous velocity at its highest point but possesses a non-zero downward acceleration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Speed is the absolute magnitude of velocity, \(|v|\). An object speeds up only when velocity and acceleration share the same algebraic sign. When velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, the speed decreases. In free projectile motion under gravity, acceleration remains constant at \(-g\) downward throughout the flight.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
If a particle moves along the negative \(x\)-axis with negative velocity (for example, \(v = -15\text{ m/s}\)) and has a positive acceleration (for example, \(a = +3\text{ m/s}^2\)), its velocity one second later is \(v = -15 + 3 = -12\text{ m/s}\). Its speed decreases from \(15\text{ m/s}\) to \(12\text{ m/s}\). Therefore, a positive acceleration does not necessarily imply speeding up. Hence, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
At the maximum height of a vertical throw, the upward velocity momentarily decreases to zero (\(v = 0\)) as the particle transitions from upward to downward motion. However, the downward gravitational force acts continuously without interruption, maintaining a constant downward acceleration of magnitude \(g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\). Thus, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
Evaluating both statements reveals that positive acceleration can cause slowing down when opposing initial velocity, making the first assertion false, while non-zero gravitational acceleration persists at momentary rest, making the second assertion true. Therefore, the first statement is incorrect but the second statement is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q04 - Area and slope interpretations of kinematic graphs

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The area bounded by a velocity–time graph and the time axis between two instants of time equals the displacement of the object over that interval.

Statement II: The slope of the tangent to a position–time graph at any specific instant gives the instantaneous velocity of the object at that instant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In one-dimensional kinematics, velocity is the time derivative of position, \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\), and displacement is the definite integral of velocity with respect to time, \(\Delta x = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
By integral calculus and geometric definition, the definite integral \(\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) corresponds to the net area under the velocity–time curve between \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), where area above the time axis contributes positively and area below contributes negatively. This net area gives the exact displacement \(\Delta x\). Thus, the first statement is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
The instantaneous rate of change of position with respect to time, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\), is geometrically represented by the slope of the tangent line drawn to the \(x\)–\(t\) curve at that time coordinate. Thus, the slope of the tangent yields the instantaneous velocity. Hence, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
Both statements describe standard, fundamental geometric representations in kinematics: area under the velocity–time graph gives displacement, and slope of the position–time graph gives instantaneous velocity. Therefore, both statements are correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q05 - Stopping distance quadratic scaling and reaction distance

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For an automobile brought to rest by constant braking retardation, the stopping distance is directly proportional to the square of its initial velocity.

Statement II: The distance traveled by a vehicle during the driver's reaction time prior to braking is directly proportional to its initial velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stopping distance \(d_s\) is the distance traveled while braking until final speed \(v = 0\). From the third equation of motion, \(0 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\), which gives \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\). Reaction time \(t_r\) is the time elapsed before brakes are engaged; during this interval the vehicle continues at uniform initial speed \(v_0\), giving reaction distance \(d_r = v_0 t_r\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
From \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\), for a fixed uniform deceleration \(a\), the stopping distance varies as the square of the initial velocity (\(d_s \propto v_0^2\)). For instance, doubling the initial speed quadruples the stopping distance. Thus, the first statement is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
During the reaction time \(t_r\), the driver has not yet applied the brakes, so the vehicle travels with constant speed \(v_0\). The distance covered is \(d_r = v_0 \cdot t_r\). For a given constant human reaction time, this distance is directly proportional to the first power of initial speed (\(d_r \propto v_0\)). Thus, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
Both statements accurately formulate the kinematics of vehicular braking: stopping distance depends quadratically on initial speed, whereas reaction distance depends linearly on initial speed. Therefore, both statements are correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q06 - Applicability of kinematic equations and average velocity

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The kinematic equation \(x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\) is applicable to rectilinear motion even when the acceleration of the body varies with time.

Statement II: For uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion, the average velocity over any time interval equals the arithmetic mean of the initial and final velocities, \(\bar{v} = \frac{v + v_0}{2}\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard kinematic formulas connecting displacement, initial velocity, acceleration, and time are derived under the express condition that acceleration \(a\) is constant. When acceleration varies with time, calculus integration \(\int v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) must be performed directly.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
If acceleration \(a = a(t)\) is not constant, \(\int a(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \neq at\), and integrating velocity does not produce \(v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\). The equation \(x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\) is strictly invalid for variable acceleration. Thus, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
For constant acceleration, the velocity–time graph is a straight line. The area of the resulting trapezoid between \(t = 0\) and \(t\) is \(x = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}t\). By definition, average velocity is \(\bar{v} = \frac{x}{t} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}\), which is precisely the arithmetic mean of initial and final velocities. Thus, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
The first statement falsely extends uniform acceleration formulas to non-uniform acceleration, whereas the second statement correctly identifies the arithmetic mean property of average velocity in uniformly accelerated motion. Therefore, the first statement is incorrect but the second statement is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q07 - Galileo law of odd numbers and total fall distance

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a body falling freely from rest under uniform gravity, the distances traversed in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio of consecutive odd integers, \(1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : \dots\).

Statement II: The total distance traversed by an object dropped from rest under uniform acceleration is directly proportional to the elapsed time \(t\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Consider an object dropped from rest under uniform downward gravitational acceleration: initial velocity \(v_0 = 0\), acceleration \(a = g\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
Let each equal time interval have duration \(\tau\). The position after \(n\) intervals is \(y_n = \frac{1}{2}g(n\tau)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{2}g\tau^2\right)n^2\). The distance fallen in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) interval is \(\Delta y_n = y_n - y_{n-1} = \left(\frac{1}{2}g\tau^2\right)[n^2 - (n-1)^2] = \left(\frac{1}{2}g\tau^2\right)(2n - 1)\). For \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\), the values of \(2n - 1\) are \(1, 3, 5, 7\). Thus, the successive distances follow the ratio \(1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : \dots\). Hence, the first statement is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
The equation of motion for total distance from rest is \(y(t) = \frac{1}{2}g t^2\). Total distance is proportional to the square of time (\(y \propto t^2\)), not to the first power of elapsed time (\(y \propto t\)). A linear relationship with time occurs only in zero-acceleration uniform velocity motion. Thus, the second statement is incorrect.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
The first statement correctly articulates Galileo's law of odd numbers, while the second statement incorrectly asserts linear time dependence for accelerated motion instead of quadratic time dependence. Therefore, the first statement is correct but the second statement is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_STATEMENT_Q08 - Physical validity of position time and speed time graphs

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A position–time graph representing the one-dimensional motion of a particle can form a closed circular loop in the \(x\)–\(t\) plane.

Statement II: A speed–time graph representing the one-dimensional motion of a body can have negative values along the vertical speed axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Time is a monotonically increasing independent variable that flows in one direction. In physical reality, a single classical particle can occupy only one spatial coordinate at any given instant. Speed is defined as the magnitude of velocity, \(|v| = \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\), which by definition cannot be negative.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Statement
If an \(x\)–\(t\) graph forms a closed loop (such as a circle or ellipse), a vertical line drawn parallel to the position axis at a given time \(t\) intersects the curve at more than one point. This would mean that the particle exists in multiple distinct locations simultaneously, and also that time reverses direction along the loop. Both are physically impossible in one-dimensional classical motion. Thus, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Statement
Speed is a scalar quantity defined as the magnitude of velocity (or rate of path length covered). While velocity in one dimension can be positive or negative depending on the direction along the coordinate axis, speed can only be positive or zero (\(\text{speed} \ge 0\)). A speed–time graph can never display negative values. Thus, the second statement is incorrect.

Step 4: Comparison and Conclusion
The first statement posits an impossible multi-valued position function in time, and the second statement contradicts the fundamental non-negative definition of speed. Therefore, both statements are incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
